solution.concept_anchor: Article 368 vs. simple majority amendment under Article 3
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students often assume all changes that affect states must proceed under Article 368, conflating the 'consultation of states' in Article 3 with the formal ratification requirement.
elimination_logic: Eliminate options that place creation or alteration of states under the Article 368 special majority procedure — Article 3 operates by ordinary simple majority in Parliament.
Eliminate options suggesting states have a veto under Article 3 — Parliament merely 'refers' the Bill to the affected state legislature for its views, which are not binding.
Confirm that Kesavananda Bharati restricted Article 368 to a 'power to amend', not plenary constituent sovereignty — distinguishing it from simple-majority legislative power used in Article 3.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: A student who knows that state interests are protected when new states are created will instinctively classify Article 3 Bills under Article 368. The trap lies in conflating 'federal significance' with 'Amendment procedure'. Article 3 Bills require only a simple majority in Parliament and the affected state legislature is merely consulted, not given a ratification right. This is one of the most reliably tested distinctions in Polity prelims.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 368 governs the formal procedure for amending the Constitution and operates in three tiers: simple majority for certain provisions (though these are technically outside Article 368 itself), special majority for most provisions, and special majority plus state ratification for federally entrenched provisions.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Creating a new state under Article 3 proceeds by an ordinary Bill passed by a simple majority in Parliament. The affected state's legislature is consulted, but this consultation is not binding and the process is not governed by Article 368 at all.
• Option (b) — Correct: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) clarified that Article 368 confers only a 'power to amend' — it does not vest Parliament with unlimited constituent sovereignty. The Basic Structure doctrine flows from this distinction.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Article 368 explicitly mentions only two procedures (special majority alone, and special majority with state ratification); the three-tier structure is operationally recognised but the text itself describes two.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Bills under Article 368 and ordinary Bills are constitutionally distinct categories; they do not share procedural steps.

Value Addition:
• Article 4 provides that laws made under Articles 2 and 3 are not deemed amendments under Article 368 — directly confirming the simple-majority route.
• The 'consultation' of states under Article 3 carries no binding force — Parliament may override the state's objection.
• Kesavananda Bharati (1973) had a 7:6 majority — the slimmest possible margin for a 13-judge bench.

solution.concept_anchor: State ratification threshold — UTs excluded, no time limit

statement_analysis.statement: Union Territories are excluded from the count when determining whether the 'not less than one-half of the States' threshold for ratification has been met.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368(2) proviso refers exclusively to 'Legislatures of States'. Union Territories do not have legislatures in the constitutional sense relevant to this provision, and they are not counted toward the one-half threshold.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 368 prescribes a seven-year time limit within which state legislatures must ratify a constitutional amendment, after which the amendment lapses.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368 imposes no time limit whatsoever on state ratification. The seven-year convention belongs to the United States Constitution (Article V practice), not to India's amendment procedure.

statement_analysis.statement: The one-half threshold in Article 368(2) refers to one-half of all States existing at the time of ratification, not one-half of States that were in existence when Parliament passed the amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: The constitutional language 'not less than one-half of the States' is computed against the States as they exist when ratification is being considered, accounting for any reorganisation that may have occurred between parliamentary passage and state ratification.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students familiar with the US Constitution's seven-year ratification convention often import that rule into the Indian context, particularly since both constitutions are compared frequently in standard textbooks.
elimination_logic: Eliminate Statement 2 immediately — Article 368 contains no time limit for ratification; the seven-year limit is an American constitutional convention, not Indian.
Confirm Statement 1 — Article 368(2) proviso says 'Legislatures of States'; Union Territories, lacking full state legislatures for this purpose, are excluded from the count.
Confirm Statement 3 — the threshold is computed against States existing at the time of ratification, making options (a) and (d) incorrect since Statement 2 is false.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the frequent cross-comparison between Indian and US amendment procedures. The seven-year limit is a well-known feature of the US Article V process (sometimes set by Congress when proposing amendments). A student who has memorised this fact in a comparative context may incorrectly attribute it to India's Article 368, particularly if questions have previously asked about 'differences from the US model'.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 368(2) requires ratification by legislatures of 'not less than one-half of the States' as a precondition — before Presidential assent — for amendments affecting federally entrenched provisions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Only full States count toward the one-half threshold. Union Territories, even those with legislatures (Delhi, Puducherry), are not 'States' for this purpose and are excluded from the denominator.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 368 prescribes no time limit for ratification. Ratification can theoretically remain pending indefinitely. The seven-year convention cited is from the US Article V process, where Congress sometimes includes a ratification deadline when proposing amendments.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The threshold is calculated against States as constituted at the time of ratification — so if a new state has been carved out between Parliament's passage and state ratification, the new count applies.

Value Addition:
• India currently has 28 States — so a minimum of 14 state legislatures must ratify.
• The USA requires three-fourths of states (38 of 50) — a significantly higher bar than India's one-half.
• Australia requires both a national majority and a majority in at least 4 of 6 states in a referendum — direct popular participation, unlike India's legislative ratification.

Provisions That Appear Federal But Do NOT Require State Ratification

solution.concept_anchor: Provisions requiring state ratification — correct identification

statement_analysis.statement: An amendment altering the procedure for electing the President of India requires ratification by not less than one-half of the state legislatures.
statement_analysis.reason: Articles 54 and 55, which govern the electoral college and voting formula for presidential election, are explicitly listed in the Article 368(2) proviso as requiring state ratification.

statement_analysis.statement: An amendment to Article 356, which governs imposition of President's Rule in a state, requires ratification because it directly affects state autonomy.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 356 is not listed in the Article 368(2) proviso. Despite its significant impact on states, it requires only a special majority in Parliament — not state ratification.

statement_analysis.statement: Any amendment to the entries in the State List of the Seventh Schedule requires ratification by state legislatures.
statement_analysis.reason: The Seventh Schedule (all three lists) is explicitly covered under the Article 368(2) proviso — any addition, deletion, or modification of entries in the State List requires state ratification.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is correct, and students who correctly identify it may stop evaluating and choose (a), missing that the question asks for the INCORRECT statement.
elimination_logic: Identify the question asks which statement is NOT correct — focus on finding the false claim.
Statement 1 is correct — Articles 54 and 55 are explicitly in the ratification list under Article 368(2) proviso.
Statement 2 is incorrect — Article 356 is not in the ratification list despite its federal significance; this is the classic UPSC trap of assuming federally impactful = ratification required.
Statement 3 is correct — the Seventh Schedule is explicitly listed; therefore the NOT correct statement is Statement 2, making option (b) correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the intuitive but wrong logic that 'if a provision affects states, it must require state ratification'. Article 356 is one of the most powerful instruments the Union can wield against states, yet it is conspicuously absent from the ratification list. The Sarkaria Commission itself flagged this anomaly and recommended including Article 356 in the ratification list — a reform that has not been implemented. Students who know the Commission's recommendation may incorrectly believe Article 356 already requires ratification.
solution.final_explanation:
The Article 368(2) proviso contains an exhaustive list of provisions requiring state ratification. The key principle is that ratification is reserved for provisions governing the federal structure itself — not merely provisions that affect states in their operation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Articles 54 and 55 governing the presidential electoral college and the proportional voting formula are explicitly in the ratification list. These are federally entrenched because states participate in electing the President.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 356 (President's Rule) requires only a special majority in Parliament. It is not in the ratification list. This is a deliberate constitutional choice — and the Sarkaria Commission's unfulfilled recommendation to include it is a popular exam distractor.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Seventh Schedule, including all three lists, requires state ratification for any amendment. The 42nd Amendment's shift of education and forests to the Concurrent List is a key historical example.

Value Addition:
• Article 312 (All India Services) also does not require state ratification — only Rajya Sabha approval by a special majority.
• Article 280 (Finance Commission) and Article 360 (Financial Emergency) similarly fall outside the ratification requirement.
• The list of ratification-required provisions can be memorised as 'FEDERAL BALANCE provisions' — those governing how the Union and States share power structurally.

solution.concept_anchor: Presidential vs. Vice-Presidential election — ratification asymmetry
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually correct, and students instinctively choose (a) without carefully testing whether R actually explains A causally.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Article 66 governs the election of the Vice-President and is NOT in the Article 368(2) ratification list; an amendment to VP election procedure requires only a special majority.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The Vice-President is elected by an electoral college comprising both Houses of Parliament sitting jointly — state legislatures have no role in the VP election.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The rationale for excluding VP election from the ratification requirement is precisely that state legislatures are not part of the VP's electoral college, so states have no structural interest to protect through ratification. R is the correct explanation of A.
Map to option (a) — Both A and R are correct and R explains A. Correct option is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here is the common student tendency to mark (b) when they correctly identify both A and R as true but doubt whether the causal link is strong enough. The causal link in this question is in fact tight: the ratification requirement for Articles 54–55 exists precisely because states participate in the presidential electoral college, and that same rationale is absent for the VP's election — making R the genuine explanation of A. Students who over-analyse the causal chain and select (b) are misled by the format's (b) option which sounds safer.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between the presidential and vice-presidential election procedures is a high-yield comparison in UPSC Prelims.

Assertion (A): Correct. Article 66 governs the VP's election and is not among the provisions listed in Article 368(2) proviso. Amending VP election procedure requires only a special majority in Parliament — not state ratification.

Reason (R): Correct. The VP's electoral college under Article 66 consists of members of both Houses of Parliament sitting in a joint session. No member of any state legislature is included. This contrasts sharply with the presidential electoral college under Article 54, which includes elected members of state legislative assemblies.

Causal relationship: R correctly explains A. The rationale for requiring state ratification for Articles 54–55 is that states directly participate in electing the President through their Legislative Assembly members. Since states have no such role in VP elections, there is no federal interest to protect, and the ratification requirement is absent. R is the correct explanation.

Value Addition:
• The President's electoral college includes elected members of Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and all State Legislative Assemblies — making it a genuinely federal institution.
• The VP is elected by a joint sitting of Parliament — purely a central process.
• The 70th Amendment (1992) added elected members of NCT Delhi and Puducherry to the presidential electoral college — this amendment itself required state ratification.

solution.concept_anchor: Amendment of Articles 73/162 vs. exercise of override under Article 249
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Parliament does gain legislative power over the subject through both Article 249 resolution and Article 368 amendment, but the mechanism, procedure, and permanence differ — a student who focuses on the outcome rather than the constitutional route will choose (a).
elimination_logic: Identify that Scenario I involves a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 249 — this is a temporary statutory override, not a constitutional amendment; no ratification under Article 368 is required.

Identify that Scenario II proposes permanently transferring a subject from State List to Concurrent List by amending the Seventh Schedule — this directly engages Article 368(2) proviso, requiring state ratification.
Eliminate option (a) — both routes are NOT procedurally identical; Article 249 needs no ratification while a Seventh Schedule amendment does.
Confirm option (c) — only Scenario II requires state ratification, while Scenario I does not, making (c) the correct answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the conflation between exercising a constitutional override power (Article 249) and formally amending the constitutional distribution of powers (Article 368 + Seventh Schedule). Both result in Parliament legislating on a State List subject, but the procedural requirements are entirely different. Students who focus on the substantive outcome — Parliament legislating on a State subject — rather than the constitutional mechanism used will incorrectly conclude both require ratification.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the critical distinction between using existing constitutional override mechanisms versus formally amending the distribution of legislative powers.

Scenario I involves Article 249: When the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by a two-thirds majority declaring that a State List subject is in the national interest, Parliament may legislate on that subject for up to one year (renewable). This is not a constitutional amendment — it is a temporary legislative measure operating within the existing constitutional framework. No ratification under Article 368 is required.

Scenario II involves amending the Seventh Schedule to permanently shift a subject from the State List to the Concurrent List. This directly alters the constitutional distribution of legislative powers. Any amendment to the Seventh Schedule requires: (i) special majority in Parliament and (ii) ratification by not less than one-half of state legislatures under Article 368(2) proviso.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The two routes are procedurally distinct.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Neither route is free from all procedural constraints — Scenario I needs a Rajya Sabha supermajority.
• Option (c) — Correct: Only Scenario II requires state ratification.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Scenario I does not require any state ratification.

Value Addition:
• Article 249 resolution lapses after one year but may be renewed; it cannot create a permanent legislative shift.
• Articles 250 and 252 are similar override provisions — none require Article 368 ratification.
• The 42nd Amendment's shift of education and forests is the canonical Seventh Schedule ratification example.

solution.concept_anchor: 99th Amendment, NJAC, SC jurisdiction, and ratification requirements
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because it correctly places NJAC with ratification but incorrectly pairs SC original jurisdiction extension under Article 138 with the ratification requirement — a student who knows the NJAC fact but is less certain about Article 138 will choose (c).
elimination_logic: Confirm A-2: The 99th Amendment altered SC and HC appointment provisions (Chapter IV Part V, Chapter V Part VI) — these are in the ratification list, so ratification was required and obtained.
Confirm B-3: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record v. Union of India (2015) struck down the NJAC on Basic Structure grounds, establishing that ratification is necessary but not sufficient.
Confirm C-4: Extending SC jurisdiction under Article 138 is done by ordinary legislation (simple majority) — it does not amend Chapter IV of Part V but operates within the existing framework.
Confirm D-1: Striking down a ratified amendment for Basic Structure violation is the Kesavananda principle, reinforced in Minerva Mills — map D to 1, confirming option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in this match-the-column is pairing C (Article 138 extension of SC jurisdiction) with ratification. Students who know that SC-related amendments generally require ratification may over-extend this rule to Article 138, which is a power Parliament exercises through ordinary legislation within an already ratified constitutional framework. The distinction between 'amending the Chapter' and 'exercising a power granted by the Chapter' is subtle but crucial.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests layered knowledge of when SC-related changes require ratification and the judicial consequences of ratified amendments.

List I–List II pairings:
• A–2 (Correct): The 99th Amendment amended Articles 124, 127, 128, 217, 222, 224, and 231 — all within Chapter IV of Part V and Chapter V of Part VI, which are explicitly in the Article 368(2) ratification list. Ratification was duly secured from a majority of states.
• B–3 (Correct): The Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) struck down the NJAC, establishing that compliance with Article 368 procedure — including state ratification — is necessary but not sufficient to immunise an amendment from Basic Structure review.
• C–4 (Correct): Parliament's power under Article 138 to extend SC jurisdiction by ordinary legislation does not amend Chapter IV of Part V — it exercises a power already granted within that Chapter. No ratification under Article 368 is needed; a simple majority law suffices.
• D–1 (Correct): The principle that even a properly ratified amendment can be struck down for violating the Basic Structure originates in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and was reinforced in Minerva Mills (1980).

The trap option C-2 (pairing Article 138 with ratification) is incorrect — Article 138 is an enabling provision for ordinary law, not a trigger for Article 368.

Value Addition:
• Kesavananda Bharati was decided by a 13-judge bench — the largest ever in Indian constitutional history.
• NJAC (2015) is the most recent high-profile example of a ratified amendment being struck down.
• Article 138 allows Parliament to confer additional original jurisdiction on the SC by ordinary law — no constitutional amendment needed.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 249 override vs. Article 368 amendment of distribution provisions

statement_analysis.statement: A Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 249 empowering Parliament to legislate on a State List subject does not constitute an amendment to the Constitution and therefore does not require ratification by state legislatures.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 249 is an exercise of an existing constitutional power — it temporarily overrides the distribution of legislative powers without altering the text of the Constitution. No Article 368 procedure, including state ratification, is triggered.

statement_analysis.statement: An amendment to Article 246, which defines the scope of Union, Concurrent, and State legislative powers, does not require state ratification because Article 246 itself is not listed in the Article 368(2) proviso.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 246 falls within Chapter I of Part XI (Articles 245–255), which governs the distribution of legislative powers. This entire Chapter is listed in the Article 368(2) proviso, so any amendment to Article 246 does require state ratification.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students might hesitate on Statement 2 and incorrectly accept it, thinking only the Seventh Schedule (not Article 246) requires ratification. The correct answer (a) requires knowing that Chapter I of Part XI is in the ratification list.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 is correct — Article 249 is a temporary override measure, not a constitutional amendment; no Article 368 ratification needed.

Evaluate Statement 2 carefully — Article 246 is within Chapter I of Part XI, which is explicitly listed in Article 368(2) proviso. The statement claims Article 246 is NOT in the ratification list — this is false.
Since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect, the answer is option (c) — Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits imprecise knowledge of the ratification list. Students who memorise only 'the Seventh Schedule requires ratification' may not recall that Chapter I of Part XI (Articles 245–255) is also listed. Since Article 246 is a prominent article that students frequently encounter, they may incorrectly believe it stands alone outside the ratification requirement. The trap is a classic scope-extension error — narrowing the ratification list to only the Seventh Schedule.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between exercising constitutional override powers and formally amending the legislative distribution framework is foundational to understanding Article 368.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 249 gives Parliament a temporary legislative competence over a State List subject when the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution in the national interest. This is not an amendment — the constitutional text is unchanged. No Article 368 procedure is engaged, and state ratification is unnecessary.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 246 is part of Chapter I of Part XI of the Constitution (Articles 245–255). The Article 368(2) proviso explicitly includes 'Chapter I of Part XI' in the ratification list. Therefore, any amendment to Article 246 — which defines the scope of legislative powers across the three lists — requires state ratification. The claim that Article 246 is not listed is factually wrong.

Value Addition:
• Articles 249, 250, 252, and 253 are all override or extension mechanisms that operate within the existing constitutional framework — none trigger Article 368 ratification.
• Chapter I of Part XI spans Articles 245–255 and covers all fundamental legislative relationship provisions between Union and States.
• Article 253 (legislation to implement international treaties) — Parliament can legislate on State List subjects under this Article without state ratification.

solution.concept_anchor: 42nd Amendment — ratification required vs. Preamble amendment

statement_analysis.statement: The 42nd Amendment (1976) shifted 'education' from the State List to the Concurrent List — this required state ratification.
statement_analysis.reason: Education was Entry 11 of the State List. Its transfer to the Concurrent List amended the Seventh Schedule, which is in the Article 368(2) ratification list. State ratification was required.

statement_analysis.statement: The 42nd Amendment's addition of the words 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity' to the Preamble required state ratification.
statement_analysis.reason: The Preamble is not listed in the Article 368(2) proviso. Amending the Preamble requires only a special majority in Parliament — not state ratification. Constitutional practice confirms this.

statement_analysis.statement: The 42nd Amendment shifted 'forests' from the State List to the Concurrent List — this required state ratification.
statement_analysis.reason: Forests (Entry 20, State List) were transferred to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment, amending the Seventh Schedule and thereby requiring state ratification.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament legislating on a State List subject under Article 252 (with consent of two or more states) requires ratification under Article 368.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 252 is an exercise of an existing constitutional power, not a constitutional amendment. No Article 368 procedure is triggered, and no state ratification is required.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Only two' is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 1 and 3 as correct may also incorrectly accept Statement 2 (Preamble amendment requiring ratification) as correct if they conflate the scale of the 42nd Amendment with ratification universality.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 — Correct: Education's transfer from State List to Concurrent List amends the Seventh Schedule, triggering the ratification requirement.
Statement 2 — Incorrect: Preamble amendment is not in the Article 368(2) proviso list; only special majority needed — eliminate this as correct.
Statement 3 — Correct: Forests' transfer is also a Seventh Schedule amendment requiring ratification.
Statement 4 — Incorrect: Article 252 is a statutory override, not a constitutional amendment; no ratification needed. Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — 'Only two', making correct option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 targets the common assumption that because the 42nd Amendment was so sweeping — shifting multiple subjects and even amending the Preamble — everything it touched required state ratification. The Preamble amendment, despite being constitutionally significant, does not fall within the Article 368(2) ratification list. Students who know the 42nd Amendment in broad strokes but not its procedural granularity will mark Statement 2 as correct, inflating their count to three and choosing option (c) instead of (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The 42nd Amendment (1976) was the most extensive constitutional amendment in Indian history and involved multiple procedural categories.

| Provision | Ratification Required? |
|---|---|
| Transfer of Education to Concurrent List | Yes — Seventh Schedule amended |
| Transfer of Forests to Concurrent List | Yes — Seventh Schedule amended |
| Preamble amendment (Socialist, Secular, Integrity) | No — not in Article 368(2) proviso |
| Article 252 legislation by Parliament | No — not a constitutional amendment |

• Statement 1 — Correct: Education (State List Entry 11 → Concurrent List) is a Seventh Schedule change requiring ratification.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Preamble is not in the ratification list. Special majority alone suffices.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Forests (State List Entry 20 → Concurrent List) similarly required ratification.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Article 252 is not an amendment — it is a consent-based statutory mechanism.

Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — 'Only two'.

Value Addition:
• The 42nd Amendment also shifted 'weights & measures' and 'administration of justice' to the Concurrent List — also requiring ratification.
• Ratification during Emergency (1976) raises legitimacy concerns — state legislatures were Congress-dominated.
• Sarkaria Commission recommended partially reversing the 42nd Amendment's centralising shifts.

solution.concept_anchor: Delimitation vs. representation of states — ratification boundary
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because changing Rajya Sabha seat allocation directly affects state representation, and students may incorrectly include Option (b) in the ratification-requiring category by associating 'delimitation' with 'representation'.
elimination_logic: Identify which three items require state ratification — any change to the allocation of Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha seats to states, any amendment to the Fourth Schedule, and any change to the constitutional formula for determining state representation.
Delimitation of constituency boundaries WITHIN a state is done under the Delimitation Act (a statute), not under Article 368. No ratification required.
Option (b) — delimitation of constituencies within a state under the Delimitation Act — is the odd one out as it does not require state ratification under Article 368.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students conflate 'representation' (how many seats a state gets) with 'delimitation' (how those seats are divided into constituencies within the state). Both relate to elections, but they operate under entirely different legal frameworks. Delimitation is a statutory process under the Delimitation Act and involves the Election Commission/Delimitation Commission — it is not a constitutional amendment at all. The trap exploits the intuitive connection between constituency boundaries and state representation.
solution.final_explanation:
State ratification is required to protect states' structural interests in the federal arrangement. Changes to how many seats a state gets in Parliament directly affect its political weight — hence ratification is required. Delimitation within a state operates at a different level.

• Option (a) — Requires ratification: Amending the Fourth Schedule to alter Rajya Sabha seat allocation is a direct change to 'representation of States in Parliament' — listed in Article 368(2) proviso.
• Option (b) — Does NOT require ratification (Odd one out): Delimitation of Lok Sabha constituencies within a state is carried out by the Delimitation Commission under the Delimitation Act. It is a statutory process, not a constitutional amendment, and does not require ratification.
• Option (c) — Requires ratification: Altering the constitutional formula determining state-wise Lok Sabha seat distribution affects 'representation of States in Parliament' under Article 368(2).
• Option (d) — Requires ratification: Any amendment changing the basis on which states' seat quotas in Parliament are determined falls within 'representation of states' — requiring state ratification.

Value Addition:
• Delimitation orders passed by the Delimitation Commission are final and cannot be challenged in any court.
• The Fourth Schedule allocates Rajya Sabha seats to states and UTs — its amendment requires state ratification.
• Qualifications for membership of Parliament (Article 84) require only a special majority — no ratification.

concepts_used: Amendment of Article 368 Itself

solution.concept_anchor: 24th Amendment — Article 368 explicitly stated Parliament's amending power
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students familiar with the 42nd Amendment's sweeping nature may assume it was responsible for explicitly articulating Parliament's amending power in Article 368, rather than the 24th Amendment which preceded it.
elimination_logic: Recall that the challenge to Parliament's unlimited amending power arose in the Golak Nath case (1967), which held Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights.
Parliament responded by passing the 24th Amendment (1971), which explicitly inserted Article 368(1) stating Parliament's power to amend the Constitution.
The 42nd Amendment came in 1976 — well after the 24th Amendment; it addressed other matters. Eliminate option (b).
The 24th Amendment itself required state ratification, as amending Article 368 — a self-entrenching provision — is in the ratification list. Confirm option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap here is between the 24th Amendment (1971) and the 42nd Amendment (1976). Both are landmark amendments, and students may remember that the 42nd Amendment was the most extensive, incorrectly assuming it was also responsible for codifying Parliament's power to amend. The 24th Amendment specifically responded to Golak Nath by adding the phrase 'notwithstanding anything in this Constitution' and inserting Article 368(1) — a precise historical sequence that is frequently tested.
solution.final_explanation:
The explicit statement of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368(1) was inserted by the 24th Amendment (1971), which was enacted to overcome the Supreme Court's ruling in I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967).

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The 42nd Amendment (1976) made many changes but did not insert Article 368(1) — that was the 24th Amendment's contribution.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The 44th Amendment (1978) reversed several 42nd Amendment changes — it did not deal with Article 368(1).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The 26th Amendment (1971) abolished privy purses — unrelated to this provision.
• Option (d) — Correct: The 24th Amendment (1971) explicitly inserted Article 368(1), stating Parliament's power to amend 'by way of addition, variation or repeal' — and as an amendment to Article 368 itself, it required and obtained state ratification.

Value Addition:
• Golak Nath (1967) held that Fundamental Rights could not be amended — this prompted the 24th Amendment.
• Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled Golak Nath but introduced the Basic Structure doctrine.
• The 24th Amendment also made Presidential assent to Amendment Bills mandatory — the President cannot withhold assent.

concepts_used: Ratification by State Legislatures — Not State Governments

solution.concept_anchor: Who ratifies — Legislature not Governor or Cabinet

statement_analysis.statement: The Governor of a State may independently grant or withhold ratification of a constitutional amendment on behalf of the State.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368(2) proviso vests ratification power in the 'Legislatures of States' — not the Governor. The Governor has no constitutional authority to independently ratify or withhold ratification of an amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: Within a state legislature, no special majority is required to pass the ratification resolution — a simple majority of members present and voting suffices.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368 does not prescribe any special majority within state legislatures for ratification. The prevailing constitutional understanding is that a simple majority of the state legislature present and voting is sufficient to ratify.

statement_analysis.statement: In states with bicameral legislatures, Article 368 constitutionally mandates that both the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council must separately pass the ratification resolution.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368(2) refers to 'Legislature of the State' without specifying that both Houses must separately ratify. Constitutional practice treats the Legislative Assembly as the ratifying chamber; the Legislative Council's separate role is not constitutionally mandated.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'All three statements' is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 2 may assume the others are equally straightforward constitutional provisions, leading them to accept all three.
elimination_logic: Eliminate Statement 1 as correct — the Governor has no independent ratification power; it is the Legislature that acts under Article 368(2) proviso.
Confirm Statement 2 — no special majority is prescribed within state legislatures; simple majority suffices.
Eliminate Statement 3 as correct — Article 368 says 'Legislature of the State', not 'both Houses'; the Legislative Council is not constitutionally mandated to separately ratify.
Only Statement 2 is correct, making option (b) the answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the assumption that a bicameral legislature would naturally require both chambers to participate in ratification, especially for something as significant as a constitutional amendment. Students may import the parliamentary approval requirement (both Houses must pass the Amendment Bill at the Centre) into state ratification, incorrectly concluding that both the Assembly and Council must ratify. The constitutional text simply says 'Legislature of the State', and practice has not imposed a bicameral ratification requirement.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 368(2) proviso specifies that ratification must come from the 'Legislatures of States' — this means the elected legislative body of the state, not the Governor, state cabinet, or necessarily both Houses where a bicameral legislature exists.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Governor's role is ceremonial in this context. Ratification is a legislative act — the Governor cannot independently grant or withhold it. The legislature votes; the outcome stands.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 368 prescribes no special majority within state legislatures for ratification. A simple majority of members present and voting is constitutionally sufficient — a significant contrast with the two-thirds supermajority required in each House of Parliament.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The phrase 'Legislature of the State' in Article 368(2) has been interpreted in practice to mean ratification by the Legislative Assembly. The Legislative Council's separate role is constitutionally ambiguous and not mandated. Six states currently have bicameral legislatures, but the practice remains uniform — only the Assembly ratifies.

Value Addition:
• States with Legislative Councils: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh.
• The state cabinet's recommendation is not a constitutional prerequisite for the legislature to consider ratification.
• If a state legislature rejects a ratification resolution, it may reconsider — there is no rule preventing a second vote.

concepts_used: Sequence of Ratification: Before or After Presidential Assent?

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional sequence — ratification precedes Presidential assent
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who correctly know the three-step process may reverse the order of ratification and Presidential assent, having memorised that 'Presidential assent is always the final step' from the ordinary Bill procedure.
elimination_logic: Recall that for provisions requiring state ratification, Article 368(2) lays down a specific sequence: Parliament passes the Bill first, then states ratify, then Presidential assent is given.
Presidential assent for ordinary Bills comes last — but for ratification-required amendment Bills, assent comes AFTER ratification, not before it.
The correct sequence is: Parliamentary passage (both Houses, special majority) → State ratification (not less than one-half) → Presidential assent.
This corresponds to option (b): P → Q → R.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who have memorised 'Presidential assent is the final act' from ordinary Bill procedure instinctively place it last in any legislative sequence. For ordinary Bills and even for special-majority amendment Bills, this is correct. The trap is that for ratification-required amendment Bills under Article 368(2), the Constitution places state ratification BETWEEN Parliamentary passage and Presidential assent. Presidential assent cannot be given before ratification is complete — reversing this order is the most common error on this sub-topic.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 368(2) prescribes a sequential procedure that differs significantly from ordinary Bill procedure for amendments requiring state ratification.

The correct sequence:
• P — Parliamentary passage: The Amendment Bill must be passed by each House of Parliament by a special majority (majority of total membership + two-thirds of members present and voting).
• Q — State ratification: The Bill must then be ratified by not less than one-half of the state legislatures. No time limit is prescribed. Ratification must be completed before the next step.
• R — Presidential assent: Only after the required number of states have ratified does the Bill proceed for Presidential assent. The President has no discretion to withhold assent (24th Amendment made assent mandatory).

This P → Q → R sequence (option b) is the constitutionally correct order.

Option (a) P→R→Q and Option (c) R→P→Q and Option (d) Q→P→R are all constitutionally incorrect. Critically, assent cannot precede ratification for provisions under the Article 368(2) proviso.

Value Addition:
• For amendment Bills NOT requiring state ratification, the sequence is simply: Parliamentary passage → Presidential assent (two steps).
• The President's assent to an amendment Bill is mandatory — unlike ordinary Bills where the President can withhold assent or return the Bill.
• If ratification is pending indefinitely, the Bill does not lapse — unlike ordinary Bills which lapse on Lok Sabha dissolution.

concepts_used: No Ratification Withdrawal — Irrevocability Principle

solution.concept_anchor: Irrevocability of state ratification — contrast with USA ambiguity
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who know that ratification is treated as irrevocable under Indian constitutional practice may incorrectly assume this is also the settled position under US constitutional law, choosing the option that calls both systems identical.
elimination_logic: Recall that Indian constitutional law treats ratification as an irrevocable legislative act — constitutional silence on withdrawal is filled by judicial interpretation that once ratified, the act is final.

Contrast with the USA where Article V's silence on withdrawal has generated genuine academic and political controversy — some states have attempted to rescind ratifications, and the legal status remains contested.
Eliminate options that allow withdrawal or that treat the Indian position as identical to the US position.
Confirm option (a) — once a state legislature ratifies under Indian constitutional practice, that ratification cannot be rescinded, even by a subsequent government of the same state.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic swap here is between India and the USA. Both constitutions are silent on ratification withdrawal, but the interpretive consequence differs. In India, judicial interpretation has firmly treated ratification as an irrevocable legislative act. In the USA, the question remains genuinely contested — some state legislatures have purported to rescind ratifications (e.g., Nebraska and Ohio on the 14th Amendment), with Congress and courts taking varying positions. A student who has studied both systems may incorrectly equate them.
solution.final_explanation:
The Constitution is silent on whether a state legislature can withdraw or rescind its ratification of a constitutional amendment once given.

• Option (a) — Correct: Under Indian constitutional practice, once a state legislature ratifies an amendment, the ratification is treated as a final, irrevocable legislative act. Judicial interpretation fills the constitutional silence on withdrawal by treating ratification as binding. A subsequent state government cannot undo its predecessor's ratification.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Indian constitutional practice does not permit withdrawal — this would introduce intolerable uncertainty into the amendment process.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The US position is not identical to India's. Article V of the US Constitution is silent on withdrawal, and the issue remains debated — some rescissions have occurred and their legal validity is contested.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: There is no time limit in Article 368 — ratification cannot 'expire', and withdrawal is not permitted.

Value Addition:
• Nebraska and Ohio attempted to rescind their ratification of the 14th Amendment (1868) — Congress ultimately counted their ratifications anyway.
• India's irrevocability principle means political transitions at the state level cannot derail ratification processes.
• Constitutional silence on ratification withdrawal is a feature India shares with the USA and Australia — but interpretive outcomes differ across jurisdictions.

concepts_used: The 99th Constitutional Amendment and NJAC — A Case Study in Ratification

solution.concept_anchor: NJAC — ratification secured but amendment struck down; ratification not sufficient

statement_analysis.statement: The 99th Constitutional Amendment, which established the National Judicial Appointments Commission, required state ratification because it amended provisions relating to the Supreme Court and High Courts.
statement_analysis.reason: The 99th Amendment altered Articles 124, 127, 128, 217, 222, 224, 224A, and 231 — all within Chapter IV of Part V and Chapter V of Part VI, which are explicitly listed in the Article 368(2) proviso. State ratification was required and obtained.

statement_analysis.statement: Once the 99th Amendment received ratification from a majority of states and obtained Presidential assent, it became immune from judicial review on the ground that the proper constitutional procedure had been followed.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court struck down the NJAC in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record v. Union of India (2015), holding that compliance with Article 368 procedure — including state ratification — does not immunise an amendment from Basic Structure review.

statement_analysis.statement: The case that struck down the NJAC established that state ratification is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the constitutional validity of an amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2015 judgment held that even a properly passed and ratified amendment can be invalidated if it violates the Basic Structure of the Constitution — procedural compliance is necessary but not sufficient.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is correct, and students who quickly identify it may select (a) thinking 'Statement 1 only is wrong' without reading the question stem carefully enough to notice it asks for NOT correct statements.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — the 99th Amendment did require and obtain state ratification as it amended SC/HC provisions listed in Article 368(2) proviso.
Statement 2 is NOT correct — the Supreme Court struck down the NJAC in 2015 despite proper ratification, establishing that procedural compliance does not confer immunity from Basic Structure review.
Statement 3 is correct — the NJAC case clarified that ratification is necessary but not sufficient.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct, making option (b) the answer — 'Statement 2 only'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits a fundamental misconception that constitutional procedure, once completed correctly, makes an amendment unchallengeable. The NJAC case is the clearest modern illustration that this is wrong. Students who know the NJAC was struck down may still incorrectly accept Statement 2 if they focus on the ratification process and not the judicial review outcome. The partial truth in Statement 2 is that proper procedure was indeed followed — but the leap to 'therefore immune from judicial review' is what makes it incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
The 99th Constitutional Amendment (2014) and its judicial fate in the NJAC case are essential study for understanding the limits of the amendment procedure.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 99th Amendment amended multiple articles within Chapters IV and V of Parts V and VI (SC and HC provisions). These chapters are explicitly in the Article 368(2) ratification list. A majority of state legislatures ratified the amendment.
• Statement 2 — NOT Correct: Procedural compliance with Article 368 — including state ratification — does not make an amendment immune from judicial review. The Supreme Court struck down the NJAC in 2015 on Basic Structure grounds, specifically holding that judicial independence (an element of the Basic Structure) was violated.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The 2015 judgment is the authoritative statement that ratification is a necessary but not sufficient condition. This principle traces back to Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and was reinforced in Minerva Mills (1980).

Value Addition:
• The NJAC judgment was decided by a 5-judge Constitution Bench — the vote was 4:1 to strike down the amendment.
• Justice Chelameshwar dissented, holding the NJAC should be retained with modifications.
• The collegium system was restored after NJAC was struck down — judges appointing judges remains the operative procedure.

solution.concept_anchor: Federally significant provisions that do NOT require ratification
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because Article 312 (All India Services) directly affects state bureaucracy and students instinctively classify it as requiring ratification, when in fact it requires only a Rajya Sabha special majority resolution — not state ratification.
elimination_logic: Recall that Article 3 (creation/alteration of states) operates by ordinary simple majority — no Article 368 procedure applies at all; affected states are consulted but have no veto.
Article 312 (All India Services) requires a Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds majority — not state ratification under Article 368.
Article 280 (Finance Commission) and Article 356 (President's Rule) are not in the Article 368(2) ratification list.

The correctly matched pair is option (a): Article 3 requires simple majority only, and Article 356 is not in the ratification list — both are federally significant provisions that do NOT require state ratification.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the 'federal significance = ratification required' conflation. All four options describe provisions with obvious federal implications. The key insight is that the Article 368(2) ratification list is exhaustive — provisions not listed do not require ratification regardless of how much they affect states. Article 3 (state reorganisation), Article 356 (President's Rule), Article 312 (All India Services), and Article 280 (Finance Commission) are all federally significant but none requires state ratification under Article 368.
solution.final_explanation:
The Article 368(2) proviso contains a closed, exhaustive list. Provisions outside this list do not require state ratification regardless of their federal significance.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: Article 3 (creation/alteration of states) proceeds by an ordinary legislative Bill passed by a simple majority in Parliament. States are merely consulted — their consent is not required. Article 356 (President's Rule) is not in the ratification list; it requires only a special majority in Parliament. Both descriptions are accurate — this is the correctly matched pair.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: Article 312 requires a Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds majority (special majority), not state ratification under Article 368.
• Option (c) — Incorrectly matched: Article 280 (Finance Commission) is not in the ratification list. It requires only a special majority. The description of 'Finance Commission composition changes requiring ratification' is false.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: Fundamental Rights amendments require only a special majority — the 24th Amendment confirmed this. They do not require state ratification.

Value Addition:
• Article 3's simple majority requirement means Parliament can redraw state boundaries over a state's objection — this is a significant departure from true federalism.
• The Sarkaria Commission recommended that Article 356 amendments be added to the ratification list — this recommendation has not been implemented.
• Article 360 (Financial Emergency) also does not require state ratification.

concepts_used: Ratification and the Basic Structure Doctrine — Intersection

solution.concept_anchor: Federal character as Basic Structure — procedural and substantive protection
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually correct, and students who quickly verify both facts without analysing the causal direction will choose (a) — mistaking correlation for explanation.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The federal character of the Constitution is recognised as an element of the Basic Structure (Kesavananda Bharati, S.R. Bommai). Even an amendment secured with full state ratification cannot destroy the federal character.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Article 368 itself requires state ratification for its own amendment — this is the 'self-entrenching' nature of the provision, meaning Parliament cannot unilaterally simplify the amendment procedure.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. A states that federalism enjoys substantive protection through the Basic Structure doctrine. R explains the procedural self-entrenchment of Article 368. These are two independent protective mechanisms — R does not cause or explain A; they are parallel protections, not causally linked.
Map to option (b) — Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here is the temptation to link two true and related facts as cause and effect. Both A and R are correct, and both relate to the protection of federalism in the amendment process. However, the Basic Structure doctrine's protection of federal character (A) derives from the Kesavananda/S.R. Bommai line of cases — it is a judicially created substantive limit. The self-entrenchment of Article 368 (R) is a procedural protection. These are independent mechanisms. R does not cause A; they are parallel. Students who see both as 'protective of federalism' will incorrectly choose (a), assuming causal connection from thematic similarity.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the distinction between the substantive protection of federalism through the Basic Structure doctrine and the procedural protection of federalism through the self-entrenching Article 368.

Assertion (A): Correct. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the Basic Structure doctrine, and S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) confirmed that federalism is an element of the Basic Structure. Even an amendment that perfectly complies with Article 368 procedure — including securing state ratification — cannot destroy the federal character of the Constitution.

Reason (R): Correct. Article 368 is listed in its own proviso as a provision requiring state ratification to amend. This makes it self-entrenching — Parliament alone cannot make the amendment procedure easier or harder without states' consent.

Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. The Basic Structure protection of federal character (A) arises from judicial interpretation, not from the procedural design of Article 368. R describes a procedural safeguard; A describes a substantive judicial limit. These are parallel, not causal.

Value Addition:
• S.R. Bommai (1994) is the definitive judgment on federalism as Basic Structure — it also curtailed arbitrary use of Article 356.
• Minerva Mills (1980) added that the limited amending power itself is a Basic Structure element.
• The recursive protection: ratification procedurally protects federalism; Basic Structure substantively protects it even if ratification is obtained.

concepts_used: Comparison with Federal Ratification in USA, Australia, and Germany

solution.concept_anchor: Comparative federal ratification — USA, Australia, Germany, India thresholds
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because it correctly places Australia with the double-majority referendum requirement but incorrectly pairs Germany with a 'three-fourths state majority', confusing the US and German models.
elimination_logic: Confirm A-3: USA requires three-fourths of states (38 of 50) — the highest threshold among the four systems. This is unambiguous.
Confirm B-1: Australia requires a double majority — a national majority in a referendum AND a majority in at least 4 of 6 states. Direct popular vote, unlike India.

Confirm C-4: Germany's Bundesrat (representing state governments) directly participates in the federal legislature. Amendments approved by two-thirds of Bundesrat members are adopted — no separate ratification step by state legislatures.
Confirm D-2: India's model — one-half threshold, simple majority within state legislatures, no time limit — is the weakest federal protection comparatively. Map D to 2, confirming option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic swap trap works between the USA and Australia. Both require supermajorities of states, and students who have memorised 'three-fourths' may incorrectly assign it to Australia. The Australian model is more distinctive — it requires a referendum (direct popular vote) with a double majority (national + state majority), which is structurally different from the US model where Congress proposes and state legislatures ratify without a popular referendum. Confusing these two systems is the primary error.
solution.final_explanation:
Comparative federal amendment procedures are a recurring UPSC theme. The four systems differ in their ratification agents, thresholds, and mechanisms.

• A–3 (USA): Article V requires ratification by three-fourths of states (currently 38 of 50). Congress proposes amendments; state legislatures (or state conventions) ratify. The highest threshold among these four systems.
• B–1 (Australia): Section 128 requires a 'double majority' — a national majority in a referendum AND a majority of votes in at least 4 of 6 states. This is the only model with direct popular participation in the ratification process.
• C–4 (Germany): The Bundesrat, which directly represents state governments in the federal parliament, participates in the amendment process. A two-thirds majority in the Bundesrat is required. There is no separate state ratification step — states are structurally integrated into the federal legislature itself.
• D–2 (India): The weakest federal protection: one-half threshold (lowest), simple majority within state legislatures, no time limit, and ratification by state legislatures (not the people directly). The Punchhi Commission recommended raising the threshold.

Value Addition:
• India has 28 states — minimum 14 must ratify.
• USA has 50 states — 38 must ratify (three-fourths).
• Australia's referendum model is the most direct democratic check on constitutional change among the four.
• Germany's Bundesrat model is called 'structural integration' of states into the federal amendment process — contrasted with India's 'sequential ratification' model.

solution.concept_anchor: Sarkaria vs. Punchhi Commission — reform recommendations on ratification

statement_analysis.statement: The Sarkaria Commission (1983–1988) recommended that the threshold for state ratification of constitutional amendments should be raised and that a specific time limit should be prescribed within which state legislatures must complete ratification.
statement_analysis.reason: It was the Punchhi Commission (2010) that recommended raising the ratification threshold and adding a time limit — not the Sarkaria Commission. The Sarkaria Commission recommended expanding the list of provisions requiring ratification (specifically including Article 356 amendments) but did not recommend altering the one-half threshold or introducing a time limit.

statement_analysis.statement: The recommendation to include amendments to Article 356 (President's Rule) within the list of provisions requiring state ratification has been made by at least one commission on centre-state relations but has not been implemented.
statement_analysis.reason: The Sarkaria Commission specifically recommended that amendments to Article 356 should require state ratification, given the provision's direct impact on state autonomy. This recommendation has not been incorporated into the Constitution through any amendment.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know both commissions made ratification-related recommendations may not precisely recall which commission recommended what, and may accept Statement 1 as applying to the Sarkaria Commission rather than the Punchhi Commission.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1 carefully — the recommendations to raise the threshold and prescribe a time limit came from the Punchhi Commission (2010), not the Sarkaria Commission (1983–1988). Statement 1 incorrectly attributes these recommendations to Sarkaria — it is false.
Evaluate Statement 2 — the Sarkaria Commission did recommend including Article 356 amendments in the ratification list. This recommendation has not been implemented. Statement 2 is correct.
Since Statement 1 is incorrect and Statement 2 is correct, the answer is option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the tendency to conflate Sarkaria and Punchhi Commission recommendations, which are often listed together in study materials under 'reform recommendations on centre-state relations'. The Sarkaria Commission recommended expanding the ratification list; the Punchhi Commission recommended raising the threshold and adding a time limit. Swapping these recommendations between the two commissions is the precise trap mechanism.
solution.final_explanation:
Two important commissions have examined centre-state relations and made recommendations specifically about the constitutional amendment ratification procedure.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Sarkaria Commission (1983–1988) recommended expanding the list of provisions requiring state ratification — specifically, that amendments to Article 356 should be included. It did NOT recommend raising the one-half threshold or introducing a time limit. These recommendations came from the Punchhi Commission (2010), which specifically called for a higher threshold and a prescribed ratification deadline.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Sarkaria Commission's recommendation to include Article 356 amendments within the ratification requirement is well documented. The provision remains outside the ratification list — the recommendation has not been acted upon by Parliament.

Since Statement 1 is incorrect and Statement 2 is correct, the answer is option (d).

Value Addition:
• Sarkaria Commission was chaired by Justice R.S. Sarkaria — its report covers a wide range of centre-state issues beyond just amendments.
• Punchhi Commission (2010) was chaired by former Chief Justice M.M. Punchhi — it made more specific structural recommendations on the ratification process.
• Neither commission's recommendations on ratification have been implemented — this distinction between 'what the law is' and 'what reformers recommend' is a high-frequency UPSC discriminator.

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional Amendment Bills do not lapse on Lok Sabha dissolution
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students apply the ordinary Bill lapse rule (Bills lapse on dissolution of Lok Sabha) to Amendment Bills, incorrectly concluding that a ratification-required amendment Bill would also lapse.
elimination_logic: Recall that the ordinary Bill lapse rule applies to Bills pending in Parliament at the time of Lok Sabha dissolution — they lapse because the Lok Sabha's unfinished business ends.
Constitutional Amendment Bills, once passed by Parliament (both Houses with special majority), are no longer pending in Parliament — they have been passed and await state ratification.
Convention and practice treat passed Amendment Bills as surviving Lok Sabha dissolution — the ratification process continues independently of Parliamentary cycles.
Confirm option (b) — the Bill does not lapse; ratification can proceed and be completed by state legislatures even after Lok Sabha has been dissolved and reconstituted.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This trap exploits the automatic application of the ordinary Bill lapse rule to Amendment Bills. Students who have memorised 'Bills lapse on dissolution of Lok Sabha' apply this rule without distinguishing between Bills pending in Parliament (not yet passed) and Bills already passed by Parliament but awaiting state ratification. Once Parliament has passed an Amendment Bill, that Bill is no longer before Parliament — the ratification stage is an independent process that continues regardless of Lok Sabha dissolution.
solution.final_explanation:
The lapse rule for ordinary Bills and the status of passed Constitutional Amendment Bills pending state ratification are governed by different principles.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: This applies the ordinary Bill lapse rule incorrectly. Constitutional Amendment Bills already passed by Parliament do not lapse upon dissolution of Lok Sabha.
• Option (b) — Correct: Once both Houses of Parliament have passed a Constitutional Amendment Bill with the requisite special majority, the Bill has completed its parliamentary stage. The ratification stage — state legislatures passing ratification resolutions — proceeds independently. Dissolution of Lok Sabha does not affect this stage, and the Bill does not lapse.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: There is no constitutional requirement that ratification must be completed within the existing Lok Sabha's term. Article 368 prescribes no time limit.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The President's assent cannot be given before ratification is complete under Article 368(2) — the sequence is Parliamentary passage → ratification → assent. The scenario in (d) is constitutionally impermissible.

Value Addition:
• Some amendment Bills have had delayed ratification across different political configurations of state governments — the absence of a time limit makes this legally permissible.
• The distinction between 'Bills pending in Parliament' (which lapse) and 'Bills passed by Parliament awaiting ratification' (which do not lapse) is subtle but constitutionally significant.
• Ordinary Bills pending in Rajya Sabha at the time of Lok Sabha dissolution also do not lapse (Rajya Sabha is a continuing house).

solution.concept_anchor: Correct identification of ratification-triggering provisions vs. non-triggers

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament proposes to amend Entry 52 of the Union List (industries controlled by the Union) to add a new category of industries — this requires state ratification.
statement_analysis.reason: Entry 52 is part of the Union List in the Seventh Schedule. Any amendment to entries in the Seventh Schedule (all three lists) is listed in the Article 368(2) proviso as requiring state ratification.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament proposes to amend Article 148 to alter the service conditions of the Comptroller and Auditor General — this requires state ratification.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 148 is not listed in the Article 368(2) proviso. It falls under Chapter V of Part V (dealing with the CAG), which is not among the ratification-required categories. A special majority suffices.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament proposes to amend Article 245 to clarify the territorial extent of Union legislative power — this requires state ratification.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 245 is within Chapter I of Part XI (Articles 245–255), which is explicitly listed in the Article 368(2) proviso as requiring state ratification.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament proposes to reduce the Rajya Sabha's quorum requirement under Article 100 — this requires state ratification.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 100 (quorum) is not listed in the Article 368(2) proviso. It is not within the 'representation of states in Parliament' category or any other ratification-listed category. Only a special majority is needed.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Only two' is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 1 and 3 may also incorrectly accept Statement 2 (CAG service conditions) as requiring ratification, thinking CAG-related provisions affect federal audit of both Union and States.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 — Correct: Union List is part of the Seventh Schedule — all three lists require ratification for any amendment.
Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 148 (CAG) is not in the ratification list; Chapter V of Part V is not the same as Chapter IV of Part V (SC-related) or Chapter V of Part VI (HC-related).
Statement 3 — Correct: Article 245 is in Chapter I of Part XI — explicitly in the ratification list.

Statement 4 — Incorrect: Article 100 (quorum) is unrelated to the 'representation of states' category and is not in the ratification list. Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — 'Only two', making option (b) correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the association between the CAG and federal fiscal oversight. The CAG audits both Union and State government accounts and thus has a clear federal dimension. Students may incorrectly conclude that amendments to the CAG's service conditions or powers would require state ratification. However, Chapter V of Part V (CAG provisions, Articles 148–151) is not listed in the Article 368(2) proviso — only Chapters IV and V of Parts V and VI (SC and HC provisions) are listed.
solution.final_explanation:
Identifying which specific constitutional provisions trigger the ratification requirement requires precise knowledge of the Article 368(2) proviso list.

• Statement 1 — Correct: All three lists in the Seventh Schedule — Union, Concurrent, and State — are in the ratification list. An amendment to any entry in any list, including Entry 52 of the Union List, requires state ratification.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 148 (CAG) falls under Chapter V of Part V. The ratification list includes Chapter IV of Part V (Supreme Court) — not Chapter V of Part V. The CAG's federal role does not place it in the ratification category.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 245 is within Chapter I of Part XI, which covers Articles 245–255 (legislative relations between Union and States). This entire Chapter is in the ratification list.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Article 100 governs voting and quorum in Parliament — it is a procedural provision for parliamentary functioning and is not within the 'representation of states' category or any other ratification-listed category.

Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — 'Only two'.

Value Addition:
• The 'representation of states in Parliament' category in Article 368(2) refers to seat allocation, not parliamentary procedure.
• Chapter IV of Part V covers Articles 124–147 (Supreme Court); Chapter V of Part V covers Articles 148–151 (CAG) — a one-chapter difference that carries major procedural consequences.
• Mnemonically: ratification = federal STRUCTURE (who legislates what, how the President is elected, how courts are constituted, how states are represented) — not institutional procedures within the Union.

solution.concept_anchor: Articles 54, 55, 58, 73, 162 — which require ratification and which do not

statement_analysis.statement: An amendment to Article 55 altering the formula for computing the value of votes in the presidential election requires ratification by state legislatures.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 55 is explicitly listed in the Article 368(2) proviso. It governs the manner of election of the President, including the proportional representation formula — any amendment requires state ratification.

statement_analysis.statement: An amendment to Article 58 altering the qualifications required to be eligible for election as President does not require state ratification — a special majority of Parliament suffices.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 58 (qualifications for Presidential candidates) is not listed in the Article 368(2) proviso. It requires only a special majority in Parliament. Only Articles 54 and 55 (electoral process) are listed, not Article 58 (eligibility).

statement_analysis.statement: An amendment to Article 162 restricting the executive power of states requires state ratification, since Article 162 is in the Article 368(2) proviso.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 162, which defines the extent of executive power of states as coextensive with their legislative power, is explicitly listed in the Article 368(2) proviso. Any amendment requires state ratification.

statement_analysis.statement: An amendment to Article 77, governing the conduct of business of the Government of India, requires state ratification because it affects executive functioning at the Union level.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 77 is not listed in the Article 368(2) proviso. It is a procedural provision governing how the Union Government's business is conducted and does not fall within any ratification-required category.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' would be correct, but students who incorrectly accept Statement 4 as true (applying the flawed reasoning that executive power articles require ratification) will choose 'all four', making (d) in this format the trap for the incorrect answer of selecting all statements.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — Article 55 is explicitly in the ratification list under Article 368(2). True.
Confirm Statement 2 — Article 58 (qualifications) is NOT in the ratification list; only Articles 54 and 55 (electoral process) are. This distinction is precise and important.
Confirm Statement 3 — Article 162 is explicitly in the Article 368(2) proviso. True.
Eliminate Statement 4 — Article 77 is a procedural article for Union Government business, not in the ratification list. Statements 1, 2, and 3 are correct, making option (c) the answer.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the key discriminating statement. Students may incorrectly reason that since Articles 54 and 55 require ratification, Article 58 — which is closely linked to presidential elections — must also require ratification. The distinction is between the electoral process (Articles 54–55: who votes and how votes are counted) and candidate eligibility (Article 58: who can stand). Only the former is in the ratification list. This entity-swap within the same cluster of articles (54, 55, 58) is a classic UPSC trap design.
solution.final_explanation:
The ratification requirement applies to specific provisions, not to an entire cluster of related articles. Even within the presidential election framework, not all articles are in the ratification list.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 55 (voting formula for presidential election) is explicitly listed in Article 368(2) proviso. States participate in the presidential electoral college, so any change to the voting formula requires their ratification.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 58 (qualifications for presidential candidates) is NOT in the ratification list. Only Articles 54 and 55 are listed — those governing the electoral process itself, not the eligibility criteria for candidates.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 162 defines state executive power as coextensive with state legislative power. It is explicitly in the Article 368(2) proviso — any amendment restricting or expanding this coextensiveness requires state ratification.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Article 77 governs the conduct of Union Government business (how decisions are authenticated, business allocated among ministers). It is not in the ratification list and requires only a special majority.

Statements 1, 2, and 3 are correct.

Value Addition:
• Article 73 (Union executive power coextensive with legislative power) — also in the ratification list, paired with Article 162.
• Article 66 (Vice-Presidential election) — NOT in the ratification list; VP electoral college excludes state legislatures.
• The 70th Amendment (1992) added NCT Delhi and Puducherry to the presidential electoral college — itself required state ratification.
